reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .411 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.69 xERA on the mound, same player, same season, and neither number is a small-sample whisper. The hitting profile is built on a 16.5% barrel rate and a 14.9% walk rate working together: he hits the ball as hard as anyone and takes pitches long enough to get to his pitch, which is why the projection lands at .396 OBP and 39 home runs across 689 plate appearances even with a 22.9% strikeout rate that would alarm you on a lesser hitter. On the mound, the 98.1 mph fastball paired with a 30.4% whiff rate produces a contact profile that keeps barrels against him at just 3.8%, and the xERA of 2.69 says the underlying quality is genuine ace-caliber rather than run-prevention fortune. The whole thing hinges on health: he's pitching again after Tommy John, and the workload of carrying both roles across a full Dodgers season is the only real threat to a profile that, if he stays on the field, resolves as the most valuable player in baseball.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power side of this profile reads like a finished product: a 95.0 mph average exit velocity, 22.4% barrel rate, and an xSLG of .617 that explains why the projected .539 SLG looks, if anything, conservative. A 17.1% walk rate against a 28.4% strikeout rate is the tension in the profile, because the discipline is genuinely elite but the swing-and-miss (a 30.7% whiff rate) means the batting average will live and die by whether pitchers keep challenging him or start going around him. If they challenge him, 41 home runs and a .393 OBP at 23 years old is a legitimate MVP-tier counting line. If the K rate stays where it is and contact doesn't develop further, you're looking at a true-outcome slugger with a floor that's still very good, just noisier than the xwOBA of .433 makes it look right now.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-seven projected home runs at age 22, and the Statcast profile backs every bit of it: 93.2 mph average exit velocity, 51.8% hard-hit rate, and a 13.6% barrel rate that clusters with the genuine power hitters in this league. A 12.8% walk rate adds real on-base value to what is already a massive power profile, and the .374 xwOBA confirms the contact quality isn't running ahead of itself. The one honest friction point is the 1st-percentile OAA, which means Tampa either has to hide him defensively or absorb the cost at third base. If they can, you're looking at a middle-of-the-order force for the next decade.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The 32-homer, 37-steal projection sits right at the edge of what feels reasonable for a 24-year-old, and the Statcast card says believe it. His hard-hit rate at 48.8% and xwOBA at .363 show genuine thump in the batted-ball mix, and his sprint speed at 29.5 ft/s is genuinely elite, the kind that turns singles into doubles and routine outs into stolen bases. The one live wire is a 35.9% chase rate that ranks near the bottom of the league, which is the thing standing between him and a truly scary offensive profile. If he closes that gap at all, the .862 OPS projection starts to look conservative; if he doesn't, the strikeouts stay loud and the walk rate gets neutralized by all the free swings.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The xwOBA sits at .474 and the xSLG at .715, both at the 100th percentile, which means the Statcast profile isn't describing a good hitter — it's describing the outer edge of what a hitter can be. His 18.9% barrel rate and 94.8 mph average exit velocity aren't flukes of batted-ball luck; they're the product of a contact quality profile that has no peers in the current data. The 14.7% walk rate keeps the on-base engine running even when the barrel isn't there, and the projection of .308/.415/1.023 with 47 home runs over 683 plate appearances is just the reasonable translation of a Statcast card that leaves almost no room to argue. The only number that isn't elite is sprint speed at 24.8 ft/s, which is fine: he's a DH and nobody needs him to be anything else.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the walk rate at 5.5%, and together those two numbers describe a pitcher who misses bats without losing the zone. His K% of 29.3 is the engine, but the command side holding up separates a true ace from a high-variance flamethrower — a 5.5% walk rate at his age, at his stuff level, earns that distinction. The whiff and chase numbers are good without being historic, which means the profile isn't built on unhittable movement alone; it's built on the combination of a 97.0 mph fastball and consistent zone presence forcing hitters into bad counts. If the walk rate climbs meaningfully over a full workload, the ERA follows it up, and you're looking at a very good number-two starter rather than the front-end piece the current Statcast profile describes.

Two to three years away, medium risk, but the shape is already doing more than a teenager at this level usually does.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics are pointed in opposite directions, and that tension defines the De La Cruz profile. His 94.6 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, his barrel rate is 15.7%, and when he makes contact the ball carries — the .484 xSLG is exactly what you'd expect from that shape. The problem is a 28.7% whiff rate that pulls hard against all of it, a strikeout rate at the 15th percentile meaning there's real damage being done to the counting stats even as the quality-of-contact numbers gleam. The projection lands on .269/.346/.484 with 26 home runs and 29 stolen bases across 624 plate appearances, which is what you get when elite raw tools coexist with swing-and-miss you can't fully fix: not a diminished player, but one leaving production on the table every week. If the whiff rate comes down even modestly, the power and speed combination pushes him into a genuinely different tier; if it doesn't, this is the player, a 26-homer, 29-steal threat who also racks up strikeouts at a pace that costs him the ceiling the exit velo says he deserves.

The contact side is messier — a 27.6% whiff rate against that .250 xBA says he's not a guy who puts the ball in play and causes problems, he earns his damage in bunches. What holds this profile together is the 11.0% walk rate, which is good enough to keep the OBP functional even when the strikeouts pile up, and a full-season projection of 30 home runs and 17 steals at 22 says the athleticism hasn't fully left yet even if the sprint speed percentile suggests it's going. reports.name: Max Clark
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 372 PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the story here. A 14% strikeout rate at AAA, translating to a projected 17.7% in the majors while most big-league hitters strike out closer to 22%, puts Clark in a profile most 21-year-olds haven't built across 372 plate appearances. The walk rate translates to 9.7%, above the big-league mean, so the .355 OBP at Triple-A is earning its keep. Power is the open question: eight home runs and a .141 ISO in the minors translating to .126 in a major-league context sits well below average, and if the gap between his hit tool and impact tool doesn't close, the ceiling tilts from everyday regular toward someone who plays every day because he doesn't hurt you rather than because he beats you. If the pop develops, the contact floor lands him as a legitimate everyday piece; if it stays quiet, 20 stolen bases and a patient bat still put him in a big-league roster conversation.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 38.6% chase rate is doing a lot of work here. reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact profile is a problem and the power is not. Walker's 94.2 mph average exit velocity sits at the 98th percentile, his xSLG is .520, and yet a 35.3% chase rate and 31.1% whiff rate are eating into what should already be a monster line. The current MLB production undersells him — an xwOBA of .374 and xBA of .287 both clear the 91st percentile, meaning the actual results have lagged the underlying quality of contact. ValuCast projects 32 home runs and an .837 OPS across a full 657 plate appearances, which is what this profile looks like when the at-bats accumulate and the sequencing smooths out. The entire profile hinges on whether he can pull that chase rate down even modestly, because at 23 with this much raw power and 29.1 ft/s underfoot, a refined zone plan turns a very good player into an elite one.

If the barrel rate recovers toward where it was in his monster years, the .361 OBP foundation turns him into a genuine middle-of-the-order threat; if it doesn't, you're looking at a high-contact, low-ceiling first baseman who ages into a productive but unremarkable regular.

The power is modest, a .443 xSLG with a 7.1% barrel rate that points toward the low-to-mid teens in home runs rather than a middle-of-the-order threat, and the .763 projected OPS reflects that gap between the contact quality and the raw thump. What Contreras actually sells is the full picture behind the plate: a catcher who almost never strikes out, makes consistent hard contact, and can handle a full lineup's worth of plate appearances, which is how 647 PA and an .OBP of .350 add up to real value even without the power profile you'd dream of at the position.

The xwOBA sits at .367 with a hard-hit rate of 47.5%, so the contact quality is there even if the whiff rate at 28.4% keeps the batting average ceiling modest. reports.name: Otto Lopez
reports.published_report: The .294 xBA is the loudest number in this profile, sitting at the 96th percentile, and it tells you the contact quality is genuine even if the raw power doesn't blow anyone away. Lopez makes the ball do that with a 13.3% strikeout rate that most middle infielders can't touch, staying in zone while keeping his chase rate at 32.8% — the swing decisions are good enough that pitchers don't have an easy path to him. The 4.9% walk rate is a real limitation; if his hit-tool softens even a little, there's no on-base floor to catch him. Still, the full-season projection of .316/.358/.476 with 26 steals is a legitimate everyday profile at second or short, and the Statcast shape says the average is the most trustworthy piece of it.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: An 18.0% chase rate at 21 years old is genuinely rare, and it shapes everything else in this profile. The underlying contact quality is soft by exit-velocity standards, 88.2 mph average and 37.6% hard-hit, but his .366 xwOBA and .446 xSLG both exceed what the raw contact numbers would suggest, because pitchers can't expand the zone against him long enough to neutralize it. The projection, .278/.382/.422 with 15 home runs and 17 steals across a near-full season, is a legitimate everyday player, and at his age the discipline is the skill most likely to carry forward rather than regress. If the exit velocity doesn't grow as he fills out physically, the ceiling stays a contact-first regular rather than a middle-of-the-order threat, but that's still a useful player at a premium position.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The disconnect between a 90th-percentile xBA and a .312 projected OBP tells you everything about what limits this profile. Bichette makes contact at an elite rate, a 18.9% whiff rate with a .285 xBA, but a 39.8% chase rate that ranks near the bottom of the league bleeds the walk column dry at 6.1%, and the gap between what he deserves to hit and what he actually gets on base defines the ceiling. The power sits in a middling zone, a 7.1% barrel rate dragging against a .429 xSLG, so the projection landing at .399 SLG and 18 home runs over 690 PA reflects the contact carrying what the raw power can't. He's a solid everyday shortstop whose floor and ceiling are closer together than the batting average flatters — a second-division regular if the chase rate doesn't improve, and only marginally better if it does.

reports.name: Kyson Witherspoon
reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 65.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The 5.10 ERA is loud, but the translation is the actual problem. Across 65.7 innings at A+, Witherspoon's stuff maps to a 7.7 K/9 against a major-league average closer to 8.6, and the walk rate translates to 4.4 at the big-league level against a context where 3.2 is ordinary, leaving a K-BB% equivalent of 10.5% when the average sits at 13.5%. The shape grades out below average across the board: a 45 on miss, 40s on command and dominance, and a floor that's relief depth if the control doesn't sharpen. The ceiling here, two to three years out, is a back-end starter, and only if the walk rate closes on the gap, because there isn't a second carrying tool to bail him out if it doesn't.

reports.name: Riley Greene
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is that two of his Statcast numbers point in opposite directions. His 24.5% chase rate and 12.9% walk rate are both elite-level discipline marks, yet he whiffs on 30.0% of swings, which undercuts the contact side of what the eye test might suggest. When he does connect, it lands hard: 91.6 mph average exit velocity, a 13.9% barrel rate, and 50.2% hard contact all cluster in the same direction, and his .365 xwOBA reflects a hitter who is earning his production rather than running on luck. The projection of .278/.366/.463 with 24 home runs over 670 plate appearances is essentially what the Statcast profile says he should be — a genuine everyday outfielder with above-average power and patience. The whole thing hinges on whether that 26.8% strikeout rate stabilizes or creeps higher, because the discipline and the damage are consistent enough to carry a plus regular, but contact frequency is the one lever that could turn him into a streaky one.

reports.name: Ozzie Albies
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile is blunt: 87.1 mph average exit velocity, a 4.1% barrel rate, 27.6% hard-hit rate — bottom-fifth of the league across the board. Yet the projection still calls for 23 home runs and a .431 SLG across 684 plate appearances, and that tension deserves a look.

The path to those numbers runs entirely through contact quality improving, or volume doing the heavy lifting a weak batted-ball profile usually can't sustain. His 13.3% strikeout rate is genuinely excellent, so he puts the ball in play constantly, and a 36.8% chase rate sitting in the 14th percentile tells you pitchers are still winning outside the zone. The projection is banking on the contact staying and the exit velocity quietly creeping back toward where it was when he hit 30.

If the hard-hit rate stays at 27.6%, you're looking at a second-division regular who helps in counting stats on a good lineup's back of the order, not a middle-of-the-fantasy-lineup second baseman.

reports.published_report: The control is the carrying tool, full stop. Melvin Hernandez posted a 1.6 BB/9 across 121.7 innings at A-ball last season, and the translated walk rate of 2.4 per nine against a major-league average of 3.2 suggests the command isn't a mirage that evaporates on translation. What doesn't survive the climb as cleanly is the strikeout side: his 7.2 K/9 at that level translates to 5.9, well short of the 8.6 major-league average, and the shape of this profile is a 19-year-old who misses bats at the bottom of the pile but runs a 1.0 WHIP on feel and location alone. If the stuff ticks and the whiff rate follows, there's a setup-reliever outcome here in two to three years; if it doesn't, the floor is a useful arm who lives off command in a bullpen role and doesn't embarrass himself doing it.
reports.report: The strike throwing is the reason to keep him on a starter track; the lack of misses leaves little margin when hitters square the ball. Back-end starter lean, with a swingman or low-leverage bullpen floor; the latest meaningful sample is from 2025, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Andre Pallante
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.74 while the projected ERA comes in at 4.08, and that gap tells you most of what you need to know: the contact management holds up, the strikeouts don't. Pallante keeps barrels down to 6.1% and holds average exit velocity to 87.7 mph, which is how a pitcher with a 17.0% K rate and a 20.6% whiff rate survives in a rotation. He doesn't miss bats, he just doesn't let hitters do damage when they make contact, and that's a narrower margin for error than the ERA suggests. If his chase rate at 26.6% doesn't climb and hitters start squaring him up at a higher rate, the contact management profile erodes faster than the strikeout numbers can compensate, leaving a backend arm pitching to contact and hoping for the best.

reports.name: Emmet Sheehan
reports.published_report: The whiff numbers are loud enough to build around: a 30.8% whiff rate and a 35.0% chase rate are both well into the upper tier of the league, and those aren't the kind of numbers that evaporate when the sample grows. The problem is a 9.9% barrel rate that undercuts all of it — when contact does land, it lands hard, and that's why the xERA sits at 3.94 while a projected 4.52 ERA tells a different story about how games actually go. He misses bats at a rate most starters would take, but the barrel suppression isn't there to finish the job. If the contact management improves even modestly, he's a useful mid-rotation piece for the Dodgers; if it doesn't, he's a strikeout-heavy arm who keeps giving up enough damage to keep his rotation grip tenuous.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is quietly elite at the skills that age well. His 13.1% walk rate pairs with a 14.0% strikeout rate, a combination that almost no one in the league can match, and the .355 xwOBA reflects genuine contact quality rather than a favorable park or a hot stretch. The barrel rate sits at just 6.6%, which is ordinary, but Ramírez has always squeezed production out of his contact shape rather than pure thump, and a projected 36 stolen bases at 33 says the legs are still part of the equation. If sprint speed continues to fade below that 27.6 ft/s, the stolen base contribution compresses and the profile leans harder on a .344 OBP to carry its fantasy value — take away the walks and you're looking at a solid-but-unspectacular corner bat.

The hit tool grade is the one thing keeping this from being a clean call.

reports.name: Chase DeLauter
reports.published_report: A 20.4% chase rate and 15.9% whiff rate, both deep into the top tier of the sport, are doing a lot of work explaining why the contact picture here is better than the raw power suggests. The xBA sits at .276, yet the barrel rate is just 6.0%, which means DeLauter is making consistent, hard contact without the loft and leverage that would push that xSLG beyond .416. The projection (.277/.347/.445) essentially believes what the contact quality says: a solid average hitter with corner-profile pop, not a masher. If the barrel rate climbs into average territory, this profile gets interesting fast; if it doesn't, what's left is a disciplined, well-above-average contact hitter who earns his keep at DH by not giving away at-bats.

reports.name: Bryan Rincon
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 310 PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here. At AA, Rincon has drawn 52 walks against just 17% strikeouts, and when you translate that plate discipline to a major-league context, the walk rate lands at 12.3% against a league baseline of 8.5%, while the strikeout rate essentially washes out at average. That combination funds a .397 OBP from a 22-year-old shortstop, and the 20 stolen bases make the on-base skill matter even more. The .217 ISO translates to .159 at the MLB level, which is above-average power without being a carrying tool, so the profile lives or dies on that approach holding as pitching gets sharper. If it does, he's a low-end everyday regular inside two years; if the zone command tightens and the walks bleed off, you're looking at a bench bat with wheels.

reports.name: Zack Wheeler
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.70 and the xwOBA against is .257, both in the 94th percentile, and those two numbers say the same thing: the surface results aren't flattering a limited profile, they're confirming a real one. His 36.3% chase rate is what makes the 29.4% strikeout rate sustainable — hitters are expanding the zone, not getting beaten inside it, which means the whiffs don't depend on pure stuff holding up. At 35, the fastball is 95.3 mph, not a weapon anymore but not a liability either, and the contact he does allow stays soft enough that the barrel rate and average exit velocity both skew in his favor. If he stays healthy in Philadelphia, a mid-season ace is the reasonable outcome; if the chase rate slips as the fastball continues to age, he becomes a durable, average-suppressing mid-rotation presence rather than a front-line one.

reports.name: Nico Hoerner
reports.published_report: Seven home runs projected across 684 plate appearances tells you everything about where the power sits, but Hoerner's game was never built around the ball leaving the yard. What's actually striking is the contact architecture: a 7.9% strikeout rate that ranks at the very top of the league, an 11.5% whiff rate that backs it up, and an xBA of .285 that reflects genuinely elite bat-to-ball skill rather than a lucky BABIP diet. The problem is that the contact is soft, 86.0 mph average exit velocity and a 0.9% barrel rate that sits near the bottom of all qualified hitters, which is why the xSLG of .362 lands well below average even as the xwOBA checks out near the middle of the league. He's a plus defensive middle infielder who makes contact almost no one can match and runs well enough at 28.3 ft/s to squeeze value from grounders, and the whole profile holds together as a useful everyday player as long as his health does, because the 684 PA projection is the real question given his track record.

reports.name: Jacob deGrom
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is right there in the contact numbers: a 34.4% whiff rate sitting next to a 44.0% hard-hit rate and an average exit velocity of 90.7 mph. That's a pitcher who misses bats at an elite level but gets hurt when hitters do connect, and the xERA of 3.44 is roughly where the two forces settle. The strikeout rate at 30.4% and a walk rate of just 5.5% mean he's still commanding the zone the way only a handful of starters can, and at 97.2 mph on the fastball there's no diminishment story yet. The honest dependency here is health, a 37-year-old coming off multiple elbow procedures, and the projection calls for meaningful innings — if he stays on the mound, a mid-rotation-to-above-average season is on the table; if he doesn't, nothing else in the profile matters.

reports.name: Cal Raleigh
reports.published_report: The barrel rate and the walks pull in one direction; the contact profile pulls hard the other way. At 11.2% barrels he generates genuine over-the-fence pop, and a 12.4% walk rate keeps him from being an automatic out even when the bat isn't there, but a 32.4% strikeout rate combined with an xBA of .177 leaves almost no margin for a batting average that already sits near the Mendoza line. The projection's .191 AVG isn't pessimism — the Statcast contact grades are historically poor, and a .287 xwOBA reflects a hitter who derives almost all his value from two skills while everything in between is below the waterline. If the strikeout rate softens even modestly, the 23 projected home runs and the walk discipline make him a functional everyday catcher; if it doesn't, he's a 525-PA lineup drain who hits .191 and you're living off the position scarcity alone.

His K% at 20.5 is below average, his BB% at 9.1 is a problem, and the whiff and chase rates are just barely above the middle of the pack. The 111.6 projected innings and 8 holds tell you what MIL actually thinks he is: a swing piece who starts when needed and works leverage spots out of the pen, not a rotation fixture. If the gap between ERA and xERA closes, and xERA usually wins that argument, what's left is a depth piece whose fastball generates average contact about as often as it doesn't.

reports.name: JJ Bleday
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the story here: 13.6% puts him in the 93rd percentile, and paired with a 23.2% chase rate that ranks 87th, Bleday is doing something most hitters can't manufacture — he earns his way on base rather than batting his way there. That discipline is why a .238 projected average still produces a .340 OBP and why the xwOBA sits at .367, well above what the raw exit velocity at 89.1 mph would suggest he should be generating. The power is distributed efficiently rather than loudly: a 10.4% barrel rate without elite average velo points to angle and selection, and the projection's 27 home runs in 524 PA follows from that shape. The floor if the plate discipline erodes is a fourth outfielder; if it holds, he's a legitimate everyday contributor in Cincinnati with a line that looks better than it photographs.

reports.name: Juaron Watts-Brown

Watts-Brown is punching out batters at 11.8 per nine across AA and A+ this year, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his K/9 at 9.1 — the bat-missing is credible over 62.7 innings, not a blip. The problem is the 4.2 walks per nine, which translates to 4.0 at the MLB level where the norm sits at 3.2, and when the command grade sits at 40 the ERA earns its 5.00. reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report: The discipline is still real: a 21.1% chase rate and 16.5% whiff rate put him in genuinely elite company for plate control, and an 11.5% walk rate is well above what most corner bats deliver. The problem is everything on the other side of contact. A 4.3% barrel rate and 87.9 mph average exit velocity are bottom-third marks, and the .356 xSLG says the power that made him a perennial All-Star has quietly left the building. That gap between elite contact decisions and weak contact quality is what the .708 projected OPS is telling you: he's working counts beautifully and then not doing much damage when he wins them. If the exit velo doesn't tick back, Bregman becomes a high-OBP, low-slug corner player, useful but not dangerous, and probably a second-division regular in terms of offensive value regardless of the lineup he's placed in.

reports.published_report: The chase rate is the lead: 16.8% puts him at the very top of the sport in pitch recognition, and the 13.4% walk rate confirms it isn't just passive taking. The contact quality backs the discipline, with a .357 xwOBA and 47.1% hard-hit rate showing he does real damage when he swings. The gap between that underlying profile and a .233 projected average is the whole tension here, and it comes down to his average exit velocity sitting at 90.9 mph — enough to hurt pitchers, not enough to override bad luck or poor batted-ball placement over a full year. If the .337 OBP holds and the power translates closer to his .458 xSLG, he's a legitimate everyday outfielder who fills a lineup spot without a hole; if the average stays suppressed and the defense (22nd percentile OAA) keeps costing him, he slides toward a well-OBP'd platoon piece with pop.

reports.name: Dansby Swanson
reports.published_report: The statcast card tells you everything you need to know about why this profile is frustrating: a 26th-percentile xwOBA sitting on top of genuinely solid contact quality. His average exit velocity checks out fine, his chase rate at 26.0% is legitimately disciplined, and his 10.5% walk rate does show up in the projection as a .300 OBP — but a 30.1% whiff rate is bleeding him out inside the zone, and a 9th-percentile xBA says the bat-to-ball problem is structural, not bad luck. The projection gives him 24 home runs and 19 steals across 597 PA, which sounds like a useful player, and it would be if a .221 average didn't make a .300 OBP the ceiling of his on-base contribution. What saves the profile from being a disappointment and nothing more is the 99th-percentile fielding; if the glove holds at that level, he earns a spot in any lineup even as a second-division offensive contributor at shortstop.
